Beállítom Az egyre eszkalálódó orosz–német konfliktus újabb lépéseként Oroszország hétfőn bejelentette, bezárják a szentpétervári német főkonzulátust. Az erről szóló jegyzékeket hétfőn adták át a moszkvai német diplomáciai misszió ideiglenes ügyvivőjének – közölték vele, hogy a kétoldalú kapcsolatok elmérgesedéséért és azok következményeiért Moszkva teljes mértékben a német kormányt tekinti felelősnek. A Reuters azt írja , a főkonzulátusnak legkésőbb szeptember 18-ig kell befejeznie a működését, a kulturális intézményeknek pedig be kell szüntetniük tevékenységüket, a kiküldetésben lévő német munkatársaknak szeptember 13-ig el kell hagyniuk Oroszországot. A két ország közötti viszony az elmúlt hetekben mérgesedett el. A német kormány szeptember 1-jén közölte, hogy megállapította , Oroszország felelős a múlt hónapban a lipcsei repülőtéren történt drónos támadási kísérletért. Augusztus elején egy közepes méretű drón repült be a repülőtér területére, amin robbanószert is találtak . Az eszköz éppen az ukránok Antonov teherszállító gépe mellé zuhant le, miután a gép szárnyának csapódott, de nem robbant fel. A drón ott ért földet, ahol a legnagyobbat robbanhat egy megtankolt repülő, így már akkor biztos volt, hogy bárki állt is a háttérben, kemény üzenetet akart küldeni . Németország a történteket nem hagyta szó nélkül, több diplomáciai választ is adnak: bezáratják a bonni orosz főkonzulátust és a Berlinben működő Orosz Ház kulturális központot, emellett pedig megszigorítják az orosz állampolgárok beutazására vonatkozó ellenőrzéseket. Vlagyimir Putyin orosz elnök súlyos hibának nevezte, hogy Németország hozzájuk kötötte a lipcsei esetet – a vádakat alaptalannak nevezték és azzal vádolták a németeket, hogy bizonyítékokat hamisítottak. Nem sokkal később orosz oldalról is érkezett diplomáciai válasz: Szergej Lavrov bejelentette , bezárják a Goethe Intézet oroszországi kirendeltségeit. A két ország közötti konfliktusról itt írtunk részletesebben. Az orosz külügyminiszter nemrég azt is mondta, a lipcsei drónincidenssel kapcsolatos vádak „nagyjából egy valódi háború kezdetét jelentik” . https://www.politico.eu/article/two-iran.text: Two Iranian men have been charged with terror offenses over an alleged plot to bomb Manchester’s Jewish community. Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, appeared in a British court on Saturday on charges of preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism. Police said the two men, who were arrested last month on the eve of the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, had received material and instructions on how to make a bomb, identified targets and carried out reconnaissance ahead of an attack on Jewish targets. Advertisement Advertisement They also said another man, likely in Iran, was in contact with them over the plot. The arrests followed a joint investigation by counter-terrorism police and the MI5 secret services. The latest charges follow Prime Minister Andy Burnham announcing there were “strong indications” that Iran was involved in a suspicious incident linked to the RAF Fairford last week, which involved three vans parked strangely and a group of hooded, masked men near the airbase. Britain’s deputy assistant commissioner for counter-terrorism Vicki Evans said the last week has “brought into sharp focus some of the wider threats being projected into the UK from Iran,” while adding the two incidents “are not connected in any way.” British Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said both men had arrived to Britain via small boats in 2020 and 2023. One had been granted asylum and the other had an asylum application pending.

It features clandestine interviews with Israeli officials on Tel Aviv rooftops. Photograph: NAZA/The Guardian View image in fullscreen A scene from NAZA, a Gaza documentary from the Guardian directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. It features clandestine interviews with Israeli officials on Tel Aviv rooftops. Photograph: NAZA/The Guardian NAZA Explainer NAZA: how and where to watch the Guardian’s acclaimed Gaza documentary Film features testimony from 24 Israeli officials involved in surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians Guardian staff Thu 12 Nov 2026 09.23 EST First published on Thu 12 Nov 2026 08.57 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Where can I watch the film? NAZA will be released in full on the Guardian’s website for free in early December. Sign up here to be notified of the exact streaming date and to be sent a link to the film when it is live. NAZA has been shown by cinemas in 47 countries and seen by more than 1.5 million people since its release last month, making it one of the most-watched documentary films with a theatrical release in 2026. The film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel but has not been screened there yet. You can watch a trailer here . View image in fullscreen Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the directors of NAZA, take questions after its UK premiere at the Ritzy cinema in south London. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian What is NAZA about? NAZA is a documentary featuring testimony from 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians during the war in Gaza. The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack. The interviewees detail the methods used by the Israeli military in Gaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential Hamas operatives, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge that the attacks would also kill their families. Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity, because of the risks involved in speaking publicly. The appearance and voices of participants in the film have been digitally altered to disguise their identities. Who is behind the film? The film was directed by the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian. It builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian magazine +972, the Hebrew-language news outlet Local Call and the Guardian newspaper between 2023 and 2025. Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors – with the Palestinians Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal – of No Other Land, which documents the destruction of Masafer Yatta, a village in the occupied West Bank targeted by Israeli forces. It won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025 . NAZA was co-produced by James Wilson and executive-produced by Jonathan Glazer, the team behind the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest. View image in fullscreen NAZA features interviews with Israeli officials who explain the targeting of presumed Hamas operatives. Photograph: NAZA/The Guardian How has it been received? NAZA has received widespread critical acclaim and is selling out in cinemas across the world. The New York Times says it is “tough to watch and impossible to ignore”, while New York Magazine describes it as “one of the most important films of our time”. In a five-star review, the Financial Times says that “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film”. The film won the special jury prize at the Venice film festival in September, where its premiere had a 25-minute ovation – a festival record. In November, it won the best political documentary from the Critics Choice Association. Why has there been an Israeli backlash? The film, its directors and their confidential sources have faced fierce attacks from the Israeli government and military. The prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of sources interviewed and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”. Netanyahu also threatened to strip Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, accusing them of treason. The Israeli military’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, said the military would “not allow soldiers to be made targets through lies and blood libels” and would use “every tool at our disposal” against the film. Far-right groups have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s family home. Some of the messages included explicit calls for violence, with one protester demanding the “death penalty for traitors”. The Israeli military claimed there were “substantial errors” in the film and that it had relied on sources who had only a partial picture of the target approval process. It said that while AI was used to help identify targets in Gaza, final decisions on strikes, and the risk of civilian casualties, were signed off by officers. In response, the team behind the film have revealed they spoke to more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war. What is NAZA: The Real Story? The Israeli government is promoting an online film project, called NAZA: The Real Story , which mimics the style of the genuine NAZA film and is hosted on a website called nazadocumentary.com. It is not the real NAZA documentary and has been misleading some viewers. Initially, the rival film’s website falsely presented itself as a promotional page for NAZA itself, naming Abraham and Szor as the directors, and listing film festivals where the documentary was to be screened. The site now appears as a platform for the rival film, which has been promoted by Israeli embassies. Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who co-created NAZA: The Real Story, describes it as an “offensive move” to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians. Szor and Abraham have addressed the backlash to their documentary. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor said.
